content: The text provided appears to be a detailed and technical compilation of references, search strategies, and study characteristics related to the diagnostic accuracy of tests for detecting hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. 1. Occult hepatitis B viral infection has been studied among blood donors in South-Eastern Nigeria, highlighting the diagnostic challenges and implications for blood safety. (Pathog Glob Health, 2014;108(5):223–8). 2. Olinger CM et al. investigated the detection of hepatitis B virus genotype E surface antigen using various immunoassays and assessed the diagnostic impact of mutations in the preS/S gene. (Med Microbiol Immunol, 2007;196(4):247–52). 3. Seremba E et al. evaluated the validity of a rapid strip assay test for detecting HBsAg in hospitalized patients in Uganda, emphasizing its diagnostic utility in resource-limited settings. (J Med Virol, 2010;82(8):1334–40). 4. Shivkumar S et al. conducted a meta-analysis of rapid point-of-care first-line screening tests for hepatitis B infection, analyzing diagnostic accuracy over a 30-year period (1980–2010). (Am J Gastroenterol, 2012;107(9):1306–13). 5. Mudawi H et al. explored overt and occult hepatitis B virus infection in adult Sudanese HIV patients, shedding light on the co-infection dynamics and diagnostic challenges. (Int J Infect Dis, 2014;29:65–70). 6. N'Dri-Yoman T et al. examined occult HBV infection in untreated HIV-infected adults in Côte d'Ivoire, emphasizing the clinical significance of co-infection. (Antivir Ther, 2010;15(7):1029–34). 7. Laperche S and the Francophone African Group for Research in Blood Transfusion assessed blood-borne virus testing and transfusion safety across the African continent, providing a multinational perspective. (Transfusion, 2013;53(4):816–26). 8. Pruett CR et al. reviewed the use of rapid diagnostic tests for transfusion infectious screening in Africa, highlighting their role in improving blood safety. (Transfus Med Rev, 2015;29(1):35–44). 9. Scheiblauer H et al. evaluated the performance of 70 hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBsAg) assays globally, using a geographically diverse panel of HBV genotypes and HBsAg subtypes. (Vox Sang, 2010;98(3 Pt 2):403–14). 10. Scheiblauer H et al. further assessed 17 CE-marked HBsAg assays for clinical sensitivity, analytical sensitivity, and detection of hepatitis B virus mutants. (J Med Virol, 2006;78 Suppl 1:S66–70). 11. Mizuochi T et al. evaluated 10 commercial diagnostic kits for detecting in vitro expressed hepatitis B virus surface antigens encoded by HBV genotypes A to H. (J Virol Methods, 2006;136(1–2):254–6). 12. Ly TD et al. analyzed the sensitivities of four new commercial hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBsAg) assays in detecting HBsAg mutant forms. (J Clin Microbiol, 2006;44(7):2321–6). 13. Moerman B et al. assessed the sensitivity of four commercial HBsAg assays for detecting wild-type and mutant forms of hepatitis B surface antigen. (Clin Lab, 2004;50(3–4):159–62). 14. Zhang R et al. investigated the risk of hepatitis B virus transmission in China, focusing on proficiency testing for HBsAg detection. (Transfus Med, 2010;20(5):322–8). 15. Martin LA et al. correlated improved HBsAg detection limits with hepatitis B virus DNA nucleic acid test yield in blood donations, demonstrating advancements in diagnostic sensitivity. (Transfusion, 2012;52(10):2201–8). 16. Austin PM compared the sensitivities and specificities of two rapid HBsAg detection methods and their relationship to a third-generation commercial enzyme immunoassay. (NZ J Med Lab Science, 2005;59(2):38–40). 17. Kuhns MC et al. examined the frequency of diagnostically significant hepatitis B surface antigen mutants, highlighting their impact on diagnostic accuracy. (J Med Virol, 2007;79 Suppl 1:S42–S6). 18. Servant-Delmas A et al. evaluated the variable capacity of 13 hepatitis B virus surface antigen assays to detect HBsAg mutants in blood samples. (J Clin Virol, 2012;53(4):338–45). 19. Hirzel C et al. assessed the performance of HBsAg point-of-care tests for detecting diagnostic escape variants in clinical samples, emphasizing their clinical relevance. (J Clin Virol, 2015;69:33–5). 20. Maylin S et al. documented short-term spontaneous fluctuations of HBV DNA levels in a Senegalese population with chronic hepatitis B, providing insights into viral dynamics. (BMC Infect Dis, 2015;15(1):154).
